Where a first-time user gets stuck

I walked JusPrin’s first launch on every path I could reach and found 23 places a newcomer is likely to misread or stall. Each orange number marks the spot on the screenshot; the same number below says what is on screen, why it confuses, and a proposed fix.

The proposals are mine and nothing is decided. The app freeze after Import is left out because another session is fixing it.

The welcome screen

  1. 1

    The only buttons are “Continue with Google” and “Continue with email”. The line under them says “New or existing account, same door.”

    A new person looks for “Sign up” or “Create account” and finds neither, so they wonder whether they need an account from somewhere else first. You flagged this one.

    ProposalLead with signing up: the email button reads “Sign up free”, with a small “Already have an account? Sign in” link under it. Both still send the same email code; only the words change.

  2. 2

    Above the three boxes: “Pick how the agent should think. Change it any time in Preferences › Agent.”

    The boxes are three ways to pay for or connect the agent, not ways of thinking. The person doesn’t know yet what the agent is, what Preferences is, or why they must choose now.

    ProposalSay what the choice is: “Sign up to use the AI agent, or skip it and just slice.”

  3. 3

    “An Expert message is 5 credits.”

    “Expert” appears nowhere else on the screen, so the person can’t tell what 500 credits buys.

    ProposalSay it in things the person does, for example “500 credits is about 100 questions to the agent”. The number needs checking against real costs.

  4. 4

    “Your own API key — Free” and “Claude Code or Claude Desktop — Free · MCP server”.

    “API key” and “MCP server” are developer words. “Free” beside them makes the 500-credit offer look like the expensive choice, and an API key isn’t free: the person pays the AI company directly.

    ProposalFold both into one quieter link, “Use your own AI account instead”, and explain the two options on the screen it opens.

Signing in with email

  1. 5

    The card asks “How do you want to sign in?” and offers a Password box with “Forgot password”. The line that tells a new person what to do, “New here? The code makes your account.”, is the smallest text on the card.

    A new person has no password. A password box suggests they should already have one.

    ProposalShow only “Email me a 6-digit code” at first, with a small “Use a password instead” link for people who set one.

Typing the emailed code

  1. 6

    “The sixth digit signs you in. Read the email on any device.”

    It reads like a riddle. It means the app signs you in as soon as you type the last digit, and you can open the email on your phone.

    Proposal“Type the code from the email. You can open it on your phone.”

  2. 7

    “Use the browser instead”.

    Nothing says what happens in the browser. It means “sign in with Google instead”.

    Proposal“Sign in with Google instead”.

Waiting for Google

  1. 8

    “Finish signing in in your browser.”

    The doubled “in” reads as a typo.

    Proposal“Finish in your browser.”

The printer step, signed in

  1. 9

    “Signed in as new@example.com · 500 credits”. Your screenshot showed the same line on the OrcaSlicer import screen.

    The person just got 500 credits, and the line doesn’t say so. “500 credits” after a dot reads like a balance they had before. You flagged this one.

    Proposal“You got 500 free credits for signing up.” with the email address on a smaller line under it.

  2. 10

    “OrcaSlicer printers in another folder? Choose the folder…”

    It shows to everyone the app found no OrcaSlicer folder for, which includes everyone who has never used OrcaSlicer.

    ProposalRemove it here. The File › Import › “Import from OrcaSlicer…” menu item covers this later, once it is built.

  3. 11

    “Skip, and JusPrin slices for a generic 0.4 mm printer until you add yours.” The code shows that Skip installs OrcaSlicer’s “Generic Klipper Printer”: a 250 × 250 mm bed and Klipper G-code.

    A Bambu or Prusa owner who skips gets G-code that may not run on their printer or fit their bed, and nothing says so.

    ProposalSay what the stand-in is: “Until you add yours, files are sliced for a 250 mm Klipper printer and may not print on other printers.”

Choosing a printer model

  1. 12

    After the model is chosen, Continue stays grey and nothing on screen says why. In my run it stayed grey for 84 seconds while the app read the printer’s filaments and plates in the background.

    The person thinks they missed a field, or that the app is broken. The Mac was heavily loaded by other builds at the time (load 21 on 12 cores), so a normal Mac is probably faster; I didn’t measure that.

    ProposalShow “Reading this printer’s settings…” with a spinner under the nozzle buttons while Continue waits.

Bringing printers from OrcaSlicer

  1. 13

    All eight printers come over together. There is no way to leave one out.

    People keep old printers in OrcaSlicer that they no longer own, and they all show up in JusPrin.

    ProposalA tick box per printer, all ticked to start.

  2. 14

    The screen doesn’t say which printer JusPrin will use after the import.

    With eight printers, the person can’t guess which one their next slice uses.

    Proposal“JusPrin starts with Bambu Lab P1S, the printer OrcaSlicer had selected.”

  3. 15

    “Start fresh”.

    It sounds like it erases something. It means “skip the import and pick my printer by hand”.

    Proposal“Choose my printer instead”.

  4. 16

    The folder path and “· 3 filaments” share one line, and the count breaks onto two lines at the far right.

    The count is easy to miss and the path means nothing to most people.

    Proposal“Also brings 3 filaments” on its own line, and the path in smaller text.

What the import brought

  1. 17

    One filament failed out of seven items, and the title says “Some settings need attention”.

    It sounds alarming, and it calls printers and filaments “settings”.

    Proposal“Imported from OrcaSlicer” as the title, with the one failure shown in its row.

  2. 18

    “Not imported · its base profile, Kingroon PLA Silk, isn’t in JusPrin”, and a “Retry failed items” button.

    “Base profile” is jargon, there is no next step, and Retry fails the same way for this reason.

    Proposal“This filament is built on Kingroon PLA Silk, which JusPrin doesn’t have.” Show Retry only for failures a retry can fix, such as a file that couldn’t be read.

  3. 19

    “OrcaSlicer’s own files were not changed.”

    It answers a worry nobody raised here. The screen before already said “OrcaSlicer keeps its own copy.”

    ProposalRemove it.

Home, not signed in

  1. 20

    The printer added a moment ago says “Not connected. No network connection is set up.”

    It reads like something went wrong while adding it.

    Proposal“Connect it to send prints straight from JusPrin” beside the Connect button, with no status word until a connection was tried.

  2. 21

    The “Set up the agent” card repeats the sign-in card but never says what the agent does or that signing up gives 500 credits.

    Someone who skipped the welcome has no reason to fill it in.

    ProposalOne line of why at the top: “Get 500 free credits and ask the agent to fix failed prints.”

Home, signed in

  1. 22

    The same 500 credits have three names: “Your first month: 500 credits” on the welcome, “500 credits” after signing in, and “First-month credits … Expires 4 Dec” here. The expiry date first appears on Home.

    People wonder whether these are different credits, and learn they expire only after signing up.

    ProposalOne name everywhere, and the expiry in the sign-up line: “You got 500 free credits, good until 4 December.”

  2. 23

    “JusPrin account · Connected”, above a printer that says “Not connected”.

    “Connected” is printer language. For an account it reads as if the account is linked to a device.

    Proposal“Signed in as new@example.com”.

How this was checked

  • A scratch copy of the current build ran with its own empty data folder and a copy of your OrcaSlicer folder. The welcome, the printer form, the OrcaSlicer list and Home after adding a printer are the real app.

**What it covers.** Someone walked JusPrin's first launch on every path they could reach and listed 23 spots where a new user is likely to misread something or get stuck. The page goes screen by screen. Each screenshot has orange numbered pins, and under it the same numbers say what's on screen, why it confuses, and a fix marked "Proposal". The page says none of the fixes are decided.

The screens, and a few example problems from each:

- **Welcome screen (1–4):** There's no "Sign up" button, only "Continue with Google / email". "Pick how the agent should think" really describes how you pay for the agent. "Expert message is 5 credits" doesn't say what "Expert" means. "API key" and "MCP server" sit next to the word "Free".
- **Email sign-in, code entry and the Google wait screen (5–8):** A password box is shown to people who have no password. "The sixth digit signs you in" reads like a riddle. "Use the browser instead" really means "sign in with Google". "Signing in in" reads like a typo.
- **Printer step (9–12):** "· 500 credits" doesn't say the credits were just given. The OrcaSlicer folder picker shows up for people who never used OrcaSlicer. Skip quietly sets up a 250 mm Klipper printer. Continue stayed grey for 84 seconds with no reason shown.
- **OrcaSlicer import and its result (13–19):** You can't leave out any of the eight printers. The screen doesn't say which printer will be used. "Start fresh" sounds like it erases something. "Some settings need attention" is alarming for one failed filament. "Retry" fails again for the same reason.
- **Home (20–23):** A printer added a moment ago says "Not connected", which looks like an error. The agent card doesn't say why to sign up. The same 500 credits go by three names, and the expiry date only shows up after sign-up. "Account · Connected" uses printer wording for an account.

The notes at the end say the welcome, printer and OrcaSlicer screens come from the real app. The sign-in and import-result screens are the real page with its state set by hand, so no accounts were created on staging. Native windows such as Preferences weren't checked. Continue on the printer step also froze the app for about 108 seconds, separate from the freeze after Import that another session is fixing.

What do you want to do with it? I can go through the screenshots, check any of the claims against the code, or start making the proposed wording changes.

Pay attention to how the initial wording was very dense and hard to understand.  If you know what I'm talking about, list a few examples and tell me how the revised version helped the users understand better.

Yes. The first-launch text was written by someone who already knew how everything worked, so it squeezes each mechanism into a few clever words. A newcomer has to rebuild the meaning from those words, and usually can't. It's the same habit your global CLAUDE.md warns against: packing a mechanism into a short phrase instead of saying what the person does and what happens.

Here are the clearest cases from the review, with the original first and the proposal second.

**"New or existing account, same door."**
This is a metaphor standing in for a fact. What it means is that the same button works whether or not you have an account, and creates one if you don't. The reader has to work out what "door" refers to.
Proposal: a "Sign up free" button with "Already have an account? Sign in" under it. A new person sees the words they were looking for and doesn't have to decode anything.

**"The sixth digit signs you in. Read the email on any device."**
This describes how the code box works on the inside: it submits when the last digit is typed. It doesn't tell the person what to do.
Proposal: "Type the code from the email. You can open it on your phone." That gives one action, and "any device" becomes a concrete one.

**"New here? The code makes your account."**
This one's compressed into a cause and effect: the code creates the account. And the one line a new person needs is the smallest text on the card.
Proposal: show only "Email me a 6-digit code" at first, so there's no password box asking them for something they don't have.

**"Pick how the agent should think."**
This metaphor hides what the choice really is: how to pay for or connect the AI.
Proposal: "Sign up to use the AI agent, or skip it and just slice." It names both options and what each one means.

**"Signed in as new@example.com · 500 credits"**
The middle dot joins two facts and drops how they relate, so "500 credits" reads like a balance the person already had.
Proposal: "You got 500 free credits for signing up." The relationship is spelled out.

**"Skip, and JusPrin slices for a generic 0.4 mm printer until you add yours."**
This one's dense in a different way: it leaves out the consequence. "Generic" hides the fact that the app sets up a 250 mm Klipper printer.
Proposal: "files are sliced for a 250 mm Klipper printer and may not print on other printers." It says what will actually happen to the person's files.

**"Not imported · its base profile, Kingroon PLA Silk, isn't in JusPrin"**
These are fragments joined by a dot, around a piece of jargon ("base profile").
Proposal: "This filament is built on Kingroon PLA Silk, which JusPrin doesn't have." It's a complete sentence in everyday words.

**"An Expert message is 5 credits."**
"Expert" is an internal label that appears nowhere else on the screen.
Proposal: describe the cost in things the person does, like "about 100 questions to the agent".

All the rewrites follow the same few moves. Each one uses full sentences instead of fragments joined by dots. It names the thing the person does, not how the system works inside. It spells out the consequence instead of hinting at it. And it uses words a newcomer already has.

One caveat: the rewrites haven't been tried on real users. When I say they're clearer, that's my judgment from reading them, not a measured result.

content.text:
Today the project has almost nothing guarding the text people see on screen. `agent-docs/jusprin/design-system.md` has one line about it ("use plain language instead of slicer jargon where possible"). The wording tests in `AgentUI/src/wording.test.ts` only check text the model reads, never the text a person reads.

**Why I think it happens.** This is my explanation, not something I've tested. The agent writing the screen knows how it works, so "The sixth digit signs you in" reads clearly to it. UI space is tight, and short phrases look polished, so the agent keeps squeezing. Then whoever reviews it, often another agent with the same knowledge, finds it clear too. A rule like "use plain language" doesn't stop this, because the writer honestly believes it already wrote plainly. So the check has to come from someone who doesn't know how the screen works.

**What I'd do, strongest first:**

1. **A cold-reader check before a screen counts as done.** Hand a fresh agent only the screenshot: no code, no spec, no chat history. For each piece of text and each button, it says in its own words what it means and what will happen if it's pressed. Then compare that with what the screen is meant to do. Any mismatch means a rewrite, and you check again. That's basically how the first-launch review found its 23 problems, so it already works in practice. It catches exactly what the writer can't see.

2. **A wording rule with real before-and-after pairs** in the "Writing UI code" section of `design-system.md`, which every UI change already has to follow. Examples teach better than principles, so use pairs from the review. Name the five patterns behind them:
   - Two facts joined by a middle dot ("Signed in as … · 500 credits").
   - Metaphors ("same door", "how the agent should think").
   - Describing how the system works instead of what the person does ("The sixth digit signs you in").
   - Internal labels ("Expert").
   - Hinting at a consequence instead of stating it ("a generic 0.4 mm printer").

   The rule itself: every line says what the person does or what happens to them, in a full sentence, in words a newcomer already has.

3. **A small automated check as a backstop.** It would flag a middle dot joining clauses, plus a short list of jargon ("API key", "MCP", "base profile"), in the Home and Agent page text. It only catches surface patterns. It can't tell that a sentence is a riddle, so it supports the first two and doesn't replace them.

These are proposals. None of them is in the repo, and I haven't measured whether they cut down on cryptic text.
So you're saying that we need to recruit editor to proofread all the designs?

No, I don't mean a person. I mean one extra agent step inside the design workflow you already run. When a design agent finishes a screen, a second agent that has never seen the code or the spec gets only the screenshot. It has to say what each line means and what each button will do. Wherever its answer differs from what the screen is meant to do, the text gets rewritten. That costs one subagent call per screen, not a new hire.

There's one honest caveat. My guess is that an agent is a weaker cold reader than a real newcomer. Models are good at decoding compressed text, so it might understand "The sixth digit signs you in" even though a person stalls on it. I haven't tested that. So the agent check would be a cheap filter, and a real first-time user would stay the final test for the screens that matter most, like first launch.

We can find out whether the agent check is good enough. I'd run a fresh agent, as the cold reader, on the original first-launch screenshots from the review and count how many of the 23 problems it catches. If it catches most of them, the step is worth adding to the design workflow. If it misses many, it isn't, and we'd need a person after all. Want me to run that test?
Okay, sounds good. Create a fresh agent as a code reader.

You are playing a first-time user of a desktop app. You know nothing about how it was built. Your job is to read ten screenshots of the app's first launch and say, honestly, what you understand and where you'd hesitate.

Background, which is all a real new user would know: you own a 3D printer and just installed JusPrin, a desktop app that prepares 3D models for printing (a "slicer"). You've opened it for the first time. The screenshots are in the order you'd meet them:

/private/tmp/claude/claude-502/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/e017b21e-f4da-471a-9b19-14e9148b503c/scratchpad/coldread/screens/screen-01.jpg through screen-10.jpg

Rules:
- Read ONLY those ten image files with the Read tool. Do not open any other file, directory, repository, web page or artifact, and do not search for anything. Using anything beyond the pictures would spoil the test.
- Read the text in the pictures literally, the way a busy newcomer would. Don't be generous: if you have to puzzle out what a line means, that counts as a problem even if you eventually work it out.
- Do not stop partway to ask questions or wait for anything; finish all ten screens in one go.

For each screen, write:
1. Every line of text and every button or link, quoted exactly, each followed by one plain sentence saying what you think it means, or for a button what you expect will happen when you press it. If you're unsure, say so and give your best guess.
2. "Where I'd hesitate": each spot that would make you stop, misread, worry, or not know what to do next. Quote the words (or describe the missing information), say what you'd likely think or do, and why. Include things the screen fails to tell you that you'd want to know at that moment.

End with a short list of the problems you'd fix first across all screens, most harmful first.

Plain prose, no tables. Be specific and quote exactly.

<result>I read all ten screens in order, as someone who owns a printer, has just installed JusPrin and knows nothing else.

## Screen 1: welcome and sign-in

**What each line says to me**

- **"JusPrin"** with an ice-cream logo: the app's name. The ice cream doesn't suggest printing to me, but it's harmless.
- **The pictures:** a clean green boat on a grid next to a photo of a stringy, failed blue-and-white boat. I take it to mean "it turns the bad print into the good one."
- **"▶ Photo credits":** opens who took the photos. I'd ignore it.
- **"The AI slicer that fixes failed prints.":** this is a slicer with AI that fixes prints that went wrong. That's clear.
- **"Show it a photo of what went wrong. The agent reads your file, your settings and your slice, changes the settings and slices again.":** I photograph a failed print, and something called "the agent" changes my settings and re-slices. "The agent" is introduced without saying what it is. I guess it's the AI.
- **"Pick how the agent should think. Change it any time in Preferences › Agent.":** I'm being asked to choose how the AI thinks. But none of the choices below are about thinking. They're about accounts and payment.
- **"Your first month: 500 credits":** signing up gives me 500 free credits for a month.
- **"An Expert message is 5 credits. Your own API key stays free.":** some messages cost 5 credits. I don't know what an "Expert message" is, whether there are cheaper ones, or what an API key is for here.
- **"Continue with Google":** signs me in with my Google account.
- **"or":** a divider between Google and email.
- **"you@example.com"** field: I type my email here.
- **"Continue with email"** (greyed out): sign in with my email once I've typed it.
- **"New or existing account, same door. Google opens your browser; email stays here.":** I had to read it twice. I think it means the same button works whether or not I have an account, Google sign-in opens a browser, and email sign-in stays inside the app.
- **"By signing in you agree to the Terms and Privacy Policy.":** the usual legal line, with links.
- **"Your own API key"** with "Free": use my own AI key instead of credits. I'm guessing it means an OpenAI-type key. It doesn't say.
- **"Claude Code or Claude Desktop"** with "Free · MCP server": no idea. Something for people who use Claude. "MCP server" means nothing to me.
- **"Just slice for now":** skip all of this and use it as a normal slicer.

**Where I'd hesitate**

- **"Pick how the agent should think."** I'd look for options about thinking style, like fast versus careful, and find sign-in boxes instead. That makes me doubt I'm reading the page right.
- **"Your first month: 500 credits."** My first worry is what happens after the month. Do I get charged automatically? Do I need a card? Nothing says whether it's free to sign up or what it costs later, so I'd hesitate before handing over my email.
- **"An Expert message is 5 credits."** I can't tell how far 500 credits goes. Is that 100 messages? Is one failed-print fix one message or twenty?
- **"Your own API key stays free."** Free compared to what? "API key" is developer jargon, and I don't know which company's key it wants.
- **"Claude Code or Claude Desktop · Free · MCP server."** This is jargon aimed at a different audience. It makes the page feel like it isn't for me.
- **"New or existing account, same door."** The odd phrasing slows me down.
- **"Just slice for now"** is small and sits at the bottom. If I'm cautious about accounts, I'd struggle to see that skipping is a normal choice. I'd also wonder whether I could still use the AI later without signing in now.

## Screen 2: after entering my email

**What each line says to me**

- The headline, description and "Pick how the agent should think" line are the same as before.
- **"How do you want to sign in?":** it's asking whether I want a code or a password.
- **"alex@example.com. Change email":** the email I typed, with a link to fix it.
- **"Email me a 6-digit code"** (main button): sends a code to my inbox.
- **"New here? The code makes your account.":** if I'm new, using the code creates my account.
- **"or"**
- **"Password"** field with **"Sign in"**: if I already have a password, I type it here.
- **"Forgot password":** the reset flow.
- **"Cancel":** go back to screen 1.
- "Your own API key", "Claude Code or Claude Desktop" and "Just slice for now" are unchanged.

**Where I'd hesitate**

- The password box appears even though I'm new and never made a password. For a moment I'd wonder whether I already have an account, maybe from an older JusPrin or Obico. It's fine once I read "New here?", but showing a password field to a brand-new email feels like I'm missing something.
- Nothing says whether choosing the code means I'll have no password later. Would I need a code every time?

## Screen 3: entering the code

**What each line says to me**

- **"Check your email.":** go to my inbox.
- **"We sent a 6-digit code to alex@example.com.":** a code is on its way to that address.
- **Six boxes:** I type the code one digit per box.
- **"The sixth digit signs you in.":** I think it means that when I type the last digit, it signs me in automatically with no button. That's a strange way to say it, and I had to work it out.
- **"Read the email on any device.":** I can check the email on my phone. Fine.
- **"Send a new code":** resends the code.
- **"Change email":** go back and fix my address.
- **"Use the browser instead":** I'm not sure. It might open a web page to sign in, or it might mean clicking a link in the email instead of typing the code. My best guess is that it opens the browser for a link-style sign-in.
- **"Cancel":** back to the start.

**Where I'd hesitate**

- **"The sixth digit signs you in."** It reads like a riddle. I might type five digits and look around for a Submit button.
- **"Use the browser instead"** is unclear. I wouldn't know whether it means Google or something else, so I'd avoid it.
- The screen doesn't say how long the code lasts, or to check my spam folder if nothing arrives. Those are the two things I'd wonder about while waiting.

## Screen 4: finishing sign-in in the browser

**What each line says to me**

- **Spinning arrows with "Finish signing in in your browser.":** a browser opened (Google, I assume), and I finish there. The "in in" reads like a typo.
- **"The app continues on its own once the browser is done.":** I don't need to click anything here afterwards.
- **"Nothing happened? Open the browser again":** reopens the browser if it didn't appear.
- **"Use an email code instead":** switch to the code method.
- **"Cancel":** stop signing in.

**Where I'd hesitate**

- **"in in"** looks like a mistake, but it's minor.
- When I'm in the browser, I don't know what to do when it says I'm done. Do I close the tab? Switch back to the app myself? The screen says the app continues on its own, but not whether I need to come back to it.

## Screen 5: which printer do I have (loading)

**What each line says to me**

- **"✓ Signed in as new@example.com · 500 credits":** I'm signed in and have 500 credits.
- **"Which printer do you have?":** pick my printer.
- **"JusPrin plans every print for your printer: its bed, its nozzle and the filament it starts with. You can add more printers later.":** it needs my printer to set things up properly, and I can add more later.
- **"Reading the printer list…":** it's loading the list of printers.
- **"Continue"** (greyed out): go on once I've chosen.
- **"Skip for now":** don't pick a printer yet.
- **"Skip, and JusPrin slices for a generic 0.4 mm printer until you add yours.":** if I skip, it uses a generic printer.
- **"OrcaSlicer printers in another folder? Choose the folder…":** if I used OrcaSlicer, I can point to where its printers are stored.
- **"Back":** goes back. To sign-in? I'm already signed in, so I'm not sure what Back would undo.

**Where I'd hesitate**

- The email says **new@example.com**, but I typed alex@example.com two screens ago. A real user who saw this would panic that they're signed into someone else's account. (This may be an artifact of how the screenshots were taken, but as a reader of the pictures I noticed it.)
- **"OrcaSlicer printers in another folder?"** If I never used OrcaSlicer, I don't know what it is. If I did, I'd wonder why my printers would be "in another folder" and how I'd know which folder that is.
- **"Back"** after a finished sign-in: I worry it signs me out.
- **"the filament it starts with"** promises a filament choice. I'd expect to be asked about filament next.

## Screen 6: printer chosen

**What each line says to me**

- The same headline and description.
- **"Brand": "Bambu Lab":** I picked my printer's maker.
- **"Model": "A1 mini":** I picked my model.
- **"Nozzle": "0.2 mm", "0.4 mm" (selected), "0.6 mm", "0.8 mm":** my nozzle size, with 0.4 chosen.
- **"Most printers ship with 0.4 mm.":** if I'm unsure, 0.4 is the safe choice. Helpful.
- **"Continue":** save this printer and move on.
- **"Skip for now"**, the generic-printer note and **"Back":** the same as before.

**Where I'd hesitate**

- **Continue still looks greyed out**, the same disabled style as on the loading screen, even though brand, model and nozzle are all filled in. I'd think I missed a required field and look for one, maybe the filament it mentioned. This is the biggest blocker on this screen. If it really is disabled, I'm stuck. If it's enabled but looks disabled, I'd still hesitate.
- The text says JusPrin plans for "the filament it starts with", but there's no filament question. Does it pick one for me, and which one?
- The "Signed in as… · 500 credits" line from the previous screen is gone. That's minor, but I'd wonder whether something reset.

## Screen 7: bring printers from OrcaSlicer

**What each line says to me**

- **"Bring your printers from OrcaSlicer?":** it found OrcaSlicer printers on my computer and offers to copy them.
- **"JusPrin copies these printers with their filaments, settings and printer connections. OrcaSlicer keeps its own copy.":** it copies them and doesn't touch OrcaSlicer. That's reassuring.
- **The list:** "Creality Ender-3 V2 Neo 0.4 nozzle - Copy", "Elegoo Neptune 3 Pro 0.4 nozzle - Copy", "Qidi X-Plus 4 0.4 nozzle - Copy", "Anycubic Kobra 3 0.4 nozzle", "Bambu Lab A1 mini 0.4 nozzle", "Creality K1C 0.4 nozzle", "MyKlipper 0.6 nozzle", "Bambu Lab P1S 0.4 nozzle". These are the eight printers it will copy.
- **"/private/tmp/claude/claude-502/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/473348c5-… · 3 filaments":** where it found them, and that there are 3 filaments.
- **"Import":** copy all eight.
- **"Start fresh":** don't copy anything.
- **"Back":** return to the printer picker.

**Where I'd hesitate**

- **The order is backwards.** I just picked my A1 mini by hand, and now I'm offered an A1 mini again. Will importing give me two A1 minis? Did my choice on the last screen count?
- **I can't choose which printers to bring.** There are no checkboxes. Most people have one or two printers, not eight. I'd hesitate to import all of them, including ones named "- Copy" that look like leftovers.
- **"Start fresh"** sounds like it might also throw away the printer I just picked, or wipe something. "Don't import" or "Skip" would be clearer.
- **The folder path** is long, cut off, and looks like an internal temporary or developer folder ("/private/tmp/claude/…"). It doesn't look like OrcaSlicer's real folder. I'd worry it's reading the wrong place.
- **"3 filaments"** is tucked at the end of the path line, oddly wrapped, with no list. Eight printers but only 3 filaments seems odd, and I can't see which ones.
- It doesn't say what "printer connections" means: network access to my printers? Passwords? I'd want to know before copying them.

## Screen 8: import results

**What each line says to me**

- **"Some settings need attention":** something went wrong with part of the import.
- **"OrcaSlicer's own files were not changed.":** my OrcaSlicer is safe.
- **"Creality Ender-3 V2 Neo 0.4 nozzle - Copy · Imported", "Elegoo Neptune 3 Pro 0.4 nozzle - Copy · Imported", "Qidi X-Plus 4 0.4 nozzle - Copy · Imported", "Bambu Lab P1S 0.4 nozzle · Imported":** these four copied fine.
- **"⚠ Kingroon PLA Silk @Qidi X-Plus 4 0.4 nozzle · Not imported · its base profile, Kingroon PLA Silk, isn't in JusPrin":** one filament couldn't be copied because something it depends on is missing.
- **"2 of 3 filaments imported":** two filaments worked and one didn't.
- **"Continue":** move on.
- **"Retry failed items":** try the failed one again.

**Where I'd hesitate**

- **Four of the eight printers are missing.** Anycubic Kobra 3, Bambu Lab A1 mini, Creality K1C and MyKlipper aren't listed at all: not imported, not failed, just gone. I'd assume they silently failed or were skipped, and I'd want to know why.
- **"Some settings need attention"** promises I can do something, but the only problem shown has no action except Retry. "Its base profile… isn't in JusPrin" is jargon. I don't know what a base profile is or how to add one.
- **"Retry failed items"** probably won't help if the cause is a missing profile. I'd click it anyway, see nothing change, and feel stuck.
- The two filaments that did import aren't named, so I can't check them.
- Nothing tells me what happens to the Qidi printer that wanted that silk filament. Can I still print with it?

## Screen 9: Home (agent not set up)

**What each line says to me**

- **"JusPrin > Home":** I'm on the main home page.
- **Gear icon:** settings.
- **"PROJECTS 0":** I have no projects yet.
- **"Drop a model or project to start":** drag a file here.
- **"STL, 3MF, STEP, OBJ, AMF, SVG or ZIP. JusPrin slices it for your Bambu Lab A1 mini.":** the file types it accepts, and it will slice for my A1 mini.
- **"+ New":** start an empty project.
- **"Open…":** pick a file from my computer.
- **"Your projects will appear here, most recent first.":** this area will list my projects.
- **"AGENT" / "Set up the agent":** set up the AI.
- **"Continue with Google", "or", "you@example.com", "Continue with email":** the same sign-in options as screen 1.
- **"New or existing account, same door. Google opens your browser; email stays here."** and **"By signing in you agree to the Terms and Privacy Policy.":** as before.
- **"Your own API key · Free"** and **"Claude Code or Claude Desktop · Free · MCP server":** as before.
- **"PRINTERS" / "Bambu Lab A1 mini" / "…":** my printer, with a menu of options.
- **"Not connected" / "No network connection is set up." / "A1 mini · 0.4 mm":** the app can't talk to the printer over the network yet. It's an A1 mini with a 0.4 nozzle.

**Where I'd hesitate**

- **I'm asked to sign in again.** Screen 5 said "Signed in as … · 500 credits", and now the AGENT box says "Set up the agent" with the whole sign-in form. I'd think the sign-in failed or was lost, and I'd lose trust that my credits exist. (If this screen is what someone who chose "Just slice for now" sees, nothing on it says so. Reading the screens in order, it looks like a regression.)
- **Only one printer is listed.** I just imported four, and only the A1 mini shows. They may be below the fold, but nothing hints at more.
- **"Not connected"** in bold looks like an error. I don't know whether I need to connect to slice. Can I still save a file and use an SD card? There's no Connect button visible on this screen to fix it.
- **"JusPrin slices it for your Bambu Lab A1 mini."** If I have several printers, how do I pick a different one for this file?

## Screen 10: Home (signed in)

**What each line says to me**

- Header, gear, "PROJECTS 0", "Drop a model or project to start", "+ New", "Open…" and "Your projects will appear here, most recent first." are the same as before.
- **"STL, 3MF, STEP, OBJ, AMF, SVG or ZIP. JusPrin asks what the part is for, then plans the print for your Bambu Lab A1 mini.":** when I open a file, it will ask what the part is for and plan around that. That's interesting and new.
- **"✓ JusPrin account · Connected":** I'm signed in.
- **"×"** on that card: closes the card, or maybe signs me out. Unsure.
- **"500 credits left":** my balance.
- **"First-month credits · 500 of 500 left":** none used yet, shown as a full bar.
- **"Expires 4 Dec":** the free credits expire on 4 December.
- **"PRINTERS" / "Bambu Lab A1 mini" / "…" / "Not connected" / "No network connection is set up." / "A1 mini · 0.4 mm":** as before.
- **"Connect…":** set up the network connection to my printer.
- **"+ Add printer":** add another printer.

**Where I'd hesitate**

- **The "×" on the account card.** I'm afraid to click it. It might sign me out or remove my account, or it might just hide the card. A cross is a risky symbol to put next to "Connected" with no label.
- **"Expires 4 Dec".** Does the account expire, or only the credits? What happens on 4 December? Will I be charged, or does the AI stop working? This is the same unanswered question from screen 1, and now there's a date on it.
- **The imported printers are still missing.** Only the A1 mini is listed, with "+ Add printer" under it. I'd conclude the import of Ender-3, Elegoo, Qidi and P1S was lost, and I'd wonder why it told me "Imported".
- **The drop-zone text changed** between screens 9 and 10 from "JusPrin slices it" to "JusPrin asks what the part is for". It's not a problem, but it shows that signing in changes behavior without saying so.
- There's no hint about the headline promise, "fixes failed prints". Nothing on Home says where I'd show it a photo of a bad print.

## What I'd fix first, most harmful first

1. **Being asked to sign in again on Home after already signing in** (screen 9 after screen 5). It makes me think sign-in failed and my 500 credits are gone.
2. **Imported printers vanishing.** Eight were offered, four reported as imported, four never mentioned, and only one shows on Home. I can't trust the import.
3. **Continue looking disabled after I've filled in brand, model and nozzle** (screen 6). It looks like I can't proceed.
4. **No answer to "what happens after the free month?"** across screens 1 and 10 ("Your first month", "Expires 4 Dec"). Not knowing whether I'll be charged stops me from signing up.
5. **The OrcaSlicer import comes after I've already picked a printer, with no way to choose which printers to bring,** and a "Start fresh" button that sounds destructive.
6. **The email changes between screens** (alex@ to new@). If that happens for real, people will think they're in the wrong account.
7. **Jargon and puzzles a newcomer has to decode:** "Pick how the agent should think" (the options aren't about thinking), "Expert message", "API key", "MCP server", "same door", "The sixth digit signs you in", "Use the browser instead", "base profile".
8. **The import failure has no way to fix it.** "Some settings need attention" offers only a Retry that likely can't help.
9. **An unlabeled "×" on the signed-in account card,** which I'd fear signs me out.
10. **Small polish problems:** "signing in in" reads like a typo, the long developer-looking folder path, "3 filaments" squeezed onto the path line, a Back link after sign-in that might undo it, and "Not connected" shown as an error with no Connect button on screen 9.</result>

2026-11-06 test: a fresh general-purpose agent got only the 10 first-launch screenshots from the "First-Launch Confusion Review" artifact (renamed screen-01..10, one line of context: "you own a 3D printer, just installed JusPrin"). Kenneth's concern behind it: design agents strongly tend to write cryptic UI text.

**Why:** the writer knows the mechanism, so its own compressed text reads clear to it; only a reader without that context sees the problem.

**How to apply:** feed the cold reader screenshots from ONE coherent path. Mixing signed-in and not-signed-in screens, or hand-set states, produced false alarms (account email changing, "asked to sign in again", imported printers vanishing). Not yet adopted as a rule in design-system.md; see [[design-source-is-claude-artifacts]].

content.text:
The cold-reader test worked well for the problem you raised. The fresh agent saw only the 10 screenshots plus one line ("you own a 3D printer and just installed JusPrin"). It found 14 of the review's 23 problems outright and 4 more in part, and it caught every case of cryptic wording.

**Problems it caught by itself:**
- "Pick how the agent should think": it went looking for thinking options and found sign-in boxes.
- "Expert message", "API key" and "MCP server": it couldn't tell what 500 credits buys, and said the jargon "makes the page feel like it isn't for me."
- "Same door": "I had to read it twice."
- "The sixth digit signs you in": it called this a riddle and said it might type five digits and then look for a Submit button.
- "Use the browser instead": it couldn't tell whether this meant Google.
- "Signing in in": it read it as a typo.
- The password box for a new email, Continue staying grey with no reason, no way to leave printers out of the import, "Start fresh" sounding destructive, the path and filament count squeezed onto one line, "base profile" and a Retry that can't help, and "Not connected" looking like an error.

**Caught in part:** the missing "Sign up" button (it flagged the wording but didn't ask for the button), which printer gets used after the import, the alarming "Some settings need attention", and the free credits (it asked about the expiry but didn't notice the three different names).

**Missed:**
- Skip quietly sets up a 250 mm Klipper printer. A reader can't know this from the screen; only the code shows it.
- "· 500 credits" doesn't say the credits were just given. It read the line correctly, so for this reader it wasn't a problem.
- "OrcaSlicer's own files were not changed" is redundant. It found the line reassuring.
- The agent card doesn't say why to sign up.
- "Account · Connected" uses printer wording for an account.

So it misses things that need knowledge from outside the screen, plus finer editorial calls. It catches the cryptic phrasing that worried you.

**New questions it raised that the review didn't have:**
- What happens after the free month: will I be charged, and do I need a card? It ranked this as a reason not to sign up.
- An unlabeled × on the signed-in account card, which it was afraid would sign it out.
- How long the code lasts, and whether to check spam.
- A Back link after sign-in that might undo the sign-in.

**False alarms, which were my fault:** I mixed screenshots from different paths into one sequence, and some of them had their state set by hand. So the agent saw the email change from alex@ to new@, got asked to sign in again on Home, and watched imported printers "vanish". In real use, the cold reader needs screenshots from one consistent path.

I saved this result to memory so a later session doesn't repeat the test. Nothing in the repo has changed.

Another Claude session sent a message:
<cross-session-message from="local_dc864a80-d727-4334-bfda-a135db6ea17f">
Kenneth asks you to add a design-guidelines doc that covers on-screen wording and how a screen gets designed and checked.

Background: the First-Launch Confusion Review (https://claude.ai/artifact/91wmdS3QU8UkzbPi1zog15) found that design agents write cryptic UI text. Examples: "New or existing account, same door.", "The sixth digit signs you in.", "Pick how the agent should think.", "Signed in as … · 500 credits". Today agent-docs/jusprin/design-system.md has no wording rule beyond one line ("use plain language instead of slicer jargon where possible"), and no doc describes a design workflow from start to finish.

What Kenneth agreed to (his words: "ok. tell the main session to do this."):
1. Keep agent-docs/jusprin/design-system.md for the visual system, unchanged in scope.

JusPrin should make advanced 3D printing feel immediate: a confident path from model to machine that removes detours without hiding control. The product should feel focused, assured, inventive, and approachable. Its voice is direct, capable, and optimistic—never cute, cryptic, or over-engineered.

- Minimum printed lockup: 32 mm.

Rules for anyone, human or agent, adding or changing a JusPrin surface. They

# JusPrin design guidelines

**Status:** Canonical guidance for `jusprin-newui` on how a screen gets designed and checked, and on the words it shows. The visual system (tokens, type, color, components, logo) lives in [Design system](design-system.md); this document does not repeat it.

Design agents tend to write on-screen text that only they can read. The agent knows how the screen works, so a line like "The sixth digit signs you in." reads clearly to it and to any reviewer who knows the same. A person opening the app for the first time has to decode it, and often can't. The First-Launch Confusion Review (https://claude.ai/artifact/91wmdS3QU8UkzbPi1zog15, 2026-11-06) found 23 places on the first launch where a newcomer would misread or stall, and most of them were wording. The rules below exist to stop that at the source and to catch what still gets through.

## How a screen gets designed and checked

1. **Start from the person.** Before drawing, write down in two or three sentences who reaches this screen, what they know at that moment, what they came to do, and what they must decide here. Every line on the screen serves one of those.
2. **Draw the whole screen, not a component alone.** A board for review is the full screen at the app's size, with the header, panes and neighbouring content the person really sees there, on the JusPrin v2 canvas (https://claude.ai/artifact/ENCtdaz7gjynfbcy4JYbWJ). Build it from the Design System artifact's coded components and the app's own markup, never by copying an older board. Repeated compositions are imported by name, as [Design handoff requirements](design-system.md#design-handoff-requirements) rule 9 says.
3. **Fill it with real strings.** Text that summarises data comes from the rule that will produce it in the app, run on real data. If only a model could write a line, say so on the board.
4. **Write every line by the wording rule below.**
5. **Run the cold-reader check on the boards** (below). Rewrite and check again until every line and button reads as intended.
6. **Show the board for review by what a person sees.** Name the screen as the person would ("the welcome screen, after typing an email"), give the canvas page it is on, and attach the picture. Board ids and builder labels mean nothing to a reviewer.
7. **Build it** following [Writing UI code](design-system.md#writing-ui-code).
8. **Check it in the running app.** Take screenshots of the built screen along one real path and run the cold-reader check again. The guards prove the code went through the tokens; only the screenshots show what the person reads.

## The cold-reader check

The writer of a screen cannot see that its text is cryptic, so the check is done by a reader who knows nothing about how the screen works.

- Start a fresh agent. Give it only the screenshots and one or two sentences a real user would know (for example: "You own a 3D printer and just installed JusPrin, a desktop app that prepares 3D models for printing."). Give it no code, spec, design notes, chat history or list of suspected problems, and rename files so their names don't hint at anything.
- Use screenshots from one coherent path, in the order a person meets them. Mixing signed-in and signed-out screens, or states set by hand, makes the reader report contradictions that no user would see.
- Ask it, for each screen, to quote every line and every button exactly, say in one plain sentence what the line means or what the button will do, and list where it would hesitate, misread, worry, or not know what to do next, including information the screen leaves out. Tell it to read literally, like a busy newcomer: a line it had to puzzle out counts as a problem even if it worked it out.
- Compare its answers with the intent written in step 1. Any line it reads differently from the intent gets rewritten, however small the gap. Its other hesitations are input to weigh, not orders.

What the check is known to catch: on 2026-11-06 a fresh agent given only the review's ten screenshots fully caught 14 of the 23 problems and partly caught 4 more. It caught every cryptic phrasing in the list. It missed problems that need knowledge from outside the screen (that Skip installs a 250 mm Klipper printer) and finer editorial calls (a redundant reassurance, one allowance under three names, "Connected" used for an account). It also raised real questions the review had not, such as what happens after the free month. It has not been compared with a real first-time user, so for the screens that matter most, such as first launch, a person remains the final test.

## Wording

Every line says what the person does or what happens to them, in a full sentence, in words a newcomer already has.

The five patterns below are what the review found most. Each pair is the text the app showed and the review's proposed rewrite; the rewrites are proposals, not yet in the app.

1. **Facts joined by a middle dot.** The dot drops how the facts relate, and the reader guesses.
   - Before: "Signed in as new@example.com · 500 credits" (reads like a balance the person already had)
   - After: "You got 500 free credits for signing up.", with the email address on a smaller line under it
2. **Metaphors.** The reader has to work out what the image stands for.
   - Before: "New or existing account, same door."
   - After: a "Sign up free" button, with "Already have an account? Sign in" under it
   - Before: "Pick how the agent should think." (the options are ways to pay for or connect the agent)
   - After: "Sign up to use the AI agent, or skip it and just slice."
3. **Describing the mechanism instead of the action.** Say what the person does, not how the screen works inside.
   - Before: "The sixth digit signs you in. Read the email on any device."
   - After: "Type the code from the email. You can open it on your phone."
4. **Internal labels.** A name the team uses, shown nowhere else on the screen, explains nothing.
   - Before: "An Expert message is 5 credits."
   - After: the cost in things the person does, for example "500 credits is about 100 questions to the agent" (check the number against real costs)
5. **Hinting at a consequence instead of stating it.** If a choice changes what the person gets, say what it changes.
   - Before: "Skip, and JusPrin slices for a generic 0.4 mm printer until you add yours."
   - After: "Until you add yours, files are sliced for a 250 mm Klipper printer and may not print on other printers."

Space on a screen is tight, and short text looks finished. That is how these lines get written. Shorten only after the full sentence passes the cold-reader check, and check again after shortening.

**What worked for files:** the [[fake-host-page-fixture]] recipe under the Playwright MCP. Copy `resources/jusprin/agent/index.html` (and `home/index.html`), inject `window.wx` + a `window.SCENES` table of full `state` payloads, serve with `python3 -m http.server`, open `agent.html?panel=printer`, switch scenes with `browser_evaluate` and save with `browser_take_screenshot` (`scale: device`, `filename` under the repo's `.playwright-mcp/`, the only allowed root; move the PNGs out and `rm -rf .playwright-mcp` afterwards so `git status` stays clean). Real printer pictures come from `resources/profiles/<Vendor>/<Model>_cover.png` as data URLs. The credential card renders from a `toolActivities` entry with `tool: 'printer_connect'`, `correlationId` = an assistant message id, state `pending` (card) or `succeeded` ("Sent"). **Window overlap trap:** when another session runs `JusPrinShellHarness --printer-live` in a loop, each run opens a 1200x800 window at the same origin (360,125) on the primary display and takes the front, so display-scope zooms and clicks land on *its* window. The first display click only focuses the window; click again. `--manual-live-agent` does not enable the fake Bambu printer, so the Bambu connect path is out of reach in manual mode.

**Why:** the walkthrough's evidence would otherwise have been lost, and a click into the other session's scripted run could have corrupted its result.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.
